definition: A system of data-manipulation rules (such as a computer's instruction set, a programming language, or a cellular automaton) is Turing complete if it can be used to simulate any Turing machine.
details: A system of data-manipulation rules (such as a computer's instruction set, a programming language, or a cellular automaton) is Turing complete if it can be used to simulate any Turing machine. This concept is used to determine the computational equivalence of different systems.

explainer.lead: A system is Turing complete if its rules can simulate any Turing machine. It matters because it expresses the computational power of a language, instruction set or automaton.

tiers.eli5: It means the system is capable of doing any calculation a computer can do, given enough time and memory.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to reason about expressiveness, for example whether a configuration language or DSL can compute arbitrary functions. A pitfall is that completeness says nothing about efficiency or practicality.
tiers.paperLevel: A system of data-manipulation rules is Turing complete if it can simulate any Turing machine; two systems are Turing equivalent if each can simulate the other. The Church–Turing thesis conjectures that anything computable by algorithm is computable by a Turing machine.

explainer.example: A cellular automaton whose rules can emulate a universal Turing machine is therefore Turing complete.
